claims.claim: It is good and healthy to question and probe deeply into the things of God.

stances.summary: Faith should not sit idle. It should go on to search and ask, because Christ said "seek and you will find". Inquiry built on faith is the best kind there is.
stances.quote: Faith, then, we say, we are to show must not be inert and alone, but accompanied with investigation. For I do not say that we are not to inquire at all.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Alexandria, c. 200. The page continues: "For Search, and you shall find, it is said" (a Scripture link sits between the words on the page). Earlier in the same chapter: "For that investigation, which accords with faith, which builds, on the foundation of faith, the august knowledge of the truth, we know to be the best." He limits it: Paul told us to avoid "foolish and unlearned questions", and no one should "demand proofs from God as from men". Book 8, chapter 1 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02108.htm) says the same more bluntly: "much less are we, who are attached to the really true philosophy, on whom the Scripture enjoins examination and investigation", and "it is impossible to find, without having sought". Book 8 is a set of logical notes that may not be a finished part of the work. Clement is the classic foil to Tertullian on this question.

stances.summary: The apostles taught the essentials plainly and left the reasons and the hows unexplained on purpose. They did it so that later lovers of wisdom would have something to dig into.
stances.quote: while on other subjects they merely stated the fact that things were so, keeping silence as to the manner or origin of their existence; clearly in order that the more zealous of their successors, who should be lovers of wisdom, might have a subject of exercise on which to display the fruit of their talents
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Alexandria, c. 220-230. The work survives mainly in the Latin of Rufinus (c. 398), who says he smoothed passages he judged unorthodox, so the wording is Rufinus's Latin in English. The Greek of Against Celsus (c. 248) says the same: Book 1, chapter 13 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm): "that it is in agreement with the spirit of Christianity, of much more importance to give our assent to doctrines upon grounds of reason and wisdom than on that of faith merely". In Book 1, chapter 9, he admits that simple faith is best for the many who have no time to study. There the pagan Celsus says some Christians keep repeating "Do not examine, but believe!" Heterodox status: Origen was never condemned in his lifetime and died after torture in the Decian persecution; some of his speculative teachings (and later Origenism) were condemned in 543 and 553.

stances.summary: Keep seeking God your whole life. Faith comes first, but its goal is understanding, and God does not hate the reason He gave us.
stances.quote: Let us therefore be thus minded, so as to know that the disposition to seek the truth is more safe than that which presumes things unknown to be known. Let us therefore so seek as if we should find, and so find as if we were about to seek.
stances.translation: Arthur West Haddan, NPNF 1st series vol. 3, 1887 (New Advent edition)
stances.original: Hoc ergo sapiamus ut nouerimus tutiorem esse affectum uera quaerendi quam incognita pro cognitis praesumendi. Sic ergo quaeramus tanquam inuenturi, et sic inueniamus tamquam quasituri. (The Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/trin9.shtml, section I 1; "quasituri" is that page's slip for "quaesituri")
stances.context: Written c. 400-420. The same passage adds "that is the right purpose which starts from faith". His clearest statement is Letter 120 to Consentius (c. 410), which has no public-domain English. Latin at https://www.augustinus.it/latino/lettere/lettera_121_testo.htm (that site's file numbers run one ahead: lettera_121 holds Letter 120): "Absit namque ut hoc in nobis Deus oderit, in quo nos reliquis animantibus excellentiores creavit. Absit, inquam, ut ideo credamus, ne rationem accipiamus sive quaeramus; cum etiam credere non possemus, nisi rationales animas haberemus." My rendering: "For God forbid that He should hate in us the very thing by which He made us more excellent than the other animals. God forbid, I say, that we should believe so as not to receive or seek a reason, since we could not even believe unless we had rational souls." Later in the same letter (3.13): "Intellectum vero valde ama" ("But love understanding greatly"). Faith still leads: Tractates on John 29.6 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701029.htm): "For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that you may understand". On the Trinity 15.2.2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130115.htm): "Faith seeks, understanding finds". Limits: Confessions 10.35 counts idle curiosity (about nature, magic, demanding signs) as a temptation. Confessions 11.12.14 refuses the old joke that God was "preparing hell ... for those who pry into mysteries", saying he would rather answer "I know not" than mock "him who asks deep things".

stances.summary: Every word used about God deserves careful study, down to the syllables. Truth is hard to hunt, so look everywhere for its tracks. But we know God by what He does, not by His essence.
stances.quote: It follows then that to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark, nor, because the questions raised are what might seem to some insignificant, are they on that account to be held unworthy of heed. Truth is always a quarry hard to hunt, and therefore we must look everywhere for its tracks.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
stances.context: Caesarea, c. 375, to his friend Amphilochius. Section 1 praises his "desire for information" and his view that "not one ought to be left without exact investigation". Basil separates honest seekers from "captious listeners and questioners" who ask only to pick a fight. His limits: Letter 234 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202234.htm): "we say that we know our God from His operations, but do not undertake to approach near to His essence." Hexaemeron, Homily 1, section 9 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/32011.htm), on what the earth rests on: "Put then a limit to your thought, so that your curiosity in investigating the incomprehensible may not incur the reproaches of Job".

stances.summary: The search for truth about God is the most precious thing a person can pursue. Christianity is the true philosophy, and it leads you to God.
stances.quote: philosophy is, in fact, the greatest possession, and most honourable before God, to whom it leads us and alone commends us; and these are truly holy men who have bestowed attention on philosophy.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 155-160 by a convert who kept the philosopher's cloak. Justin is speaking in his own voice as a Christian. In chapter 1 the Jewish Trypho asks: "Is not this truly the duty of philosophy, to investigate the Deity?" Justin answers: "Assuredly, so we too have believed." First Apology 2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm): "Reason directs those who are truly pious and philosophical to honour and love only what is true, declining to follow traditional opinions, if these be worthless." In chapters 3-7 an old man shows him that philosophy alone cannot see God and that he must read the prophets. In chapter 8 he says of the prophets' teaching: "I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable. Thus, and for this reason, I am a philosopher." So the search is good, but it is finished by revelation.

stances.summary: In the matter your whole life turns on, think for yourself. God gave wisdom to everyone, so weigh the truth yourself instead of following your ancestors like sheep.
stances.quote: It is therefore right, especially in a matter on which the whole plan of life turns, that every one should place confidence in himself, and use his own judgment and individual capacity for the investigation and weighing of the truth, rather than through confidence in others to be deceived by their errors, as though he himself were without understanding.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 303-311 during and after the Great Persecution, aimed at pagans who defend their gods because "the ancients have handed them down". The chapter goes on: "since wisdom — that is, the inquiry after truth— is natural to all, they deprive themselves of wisdom, who without any judgment approve of the discoveries of their ancestors, and like sheep are led by others." His limit, earlier in Book 2: "man by himself cannot attain to this knowledge, unless he is taught by God."

stances.summary: Anyone at all may ask about God, think it through and say what they think. What matters is whether the argument is true, not how learned the person is.
stances.quote: Therefore it is nothing to be angry or to be grieved about, though any one should inquire, should think, should utter his thoughts about divine things; since what is wanted is not the authority of the arguer, but the truth of the argument itself
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 4, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: A Latin dialogue by the Roman lawyer Minucius Felix, c. 200-240. The Christian Octavius answers the pagan Caecilius, who had argued (chapters 5 and 12-13) that unlearned Christians have no right to dispute about divine things, and quoted Socrates: "What is above us is nothing to us." That is the pagan's view, not a Christian one. Octavius says all people are born "with a capacity and ability of reasoning". In chapter 17 he adds that we "have neither right nor reason to be ignorant of the celestial glory".

stances.summary: Live inside the Scriptures, meditate on them and seek nothing else. Study with a teacher, as a fellow student.
stances.quote: I beg of you, my dear brother, to live among these books, to meditate upon them, to know nothing else, to seek nothing else. Does not such a life seem to you a foretaste of heaven here on earth?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Bethlehem, c. 394. The letter goes on: "I readily pledge myself to be a fellow-student ... Let us learn upon earth that knowledge which will continue with us in heaven." His probing is into Scripture, with a guide. He spent decades answering hard questions by letter. From 393 he fought bitterly against Origen's speculative theology, so he did not approve every kind of probing.

stances.summary: The hardest questions about God deserve long thought, with every bit of reason God has given. But reason can only climb so high, and the subject is for the few.
stances.quote: I HAVE long pondered this problem with such mind as I have and all the light that God has lent me.
stances.translation: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, Loeb Classical Library, 1918
stances.original: Investigatam diutissime quaestionem, quantum nostrae mentis igniculum lux diuina dignata est, formatam rationibus litterisque mandatam offerendam uobis communicandamque curaui (Loeb facing Latin, same OCR file; the OCR reads "INVESTIGATAM diutissime quaestionern, quantum nos- trae mentis")
stances.work: Theological Tractates: On the Trinity (De Trinitate)
stances.context: Rome, c. 520; executed c. 524-525. The page is an OCR text; the Loeb prints the first words in capitals ("I HAVE"). The same preface sets a limit: "We should not of course press our inquiry further than man's wit and reason are allowed to climb the height of heavenly knowledge." He also writes in "new and unaccustomed words" so that only Symmachus will understand, since the crowd would trample it. The learning topic already uses his line "reconcile faith and reason".

stances.summary: Doubts should be put on the table and answered. State the opposing case as strongly as you can, and then look for the truth together.
stances.quote: we must seek where we may get a beginning for our discussion upon this point; and if you please, let the defense of the opposing views be undertaken by yourself; for I see that your mind is a little inclined to accept such a brief. Then, after the conflicting belief has been stated, we shall be able to look for the truth.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection, by Gregory of Nyssa
stances.location: Opening of the dialogue (Macrina, called "the Teacher", speaking)
stances.context: Gregory of Nyssa wrote this dialogue c. 380-381, set at his sister's deathbed in 379. Her words are his literary record of her teaching, not a transcript. She has her grieving brother argue against the soul's survival so they can test it. Her limits: she asks to be excused from "the rule of dialectic", calling it "a weak and questionable way of demonstrating truth". She takes Scripture as the rule. When he raises doubts that God exists at all, she says "It would be more fitting ... to be silent about such doubts", then answers them anyway from creation.

stances.summary: Study God's ways within the faith you were taught, and you will learn much. But some answers belong to God alone, and we should be content to leave them with Him.
stances.quote: we are able by the grace of God to explain some of them, while we must leave others in the hands of God, and that not only in the present world, but also in that which is to come, so that God should for ever teach, and man should for ever learn the things taught him by God?
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Lyons, c. 180, against Gnostic speculation. The same chapter (section 1) encourages inquiry: "it is much more suitable that we, directing our inquiries after this fashion, should exercise ourselves in the investigation of the mystery and administration of the living God". Book 1, chapter 10, section 3 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103110.htm) lists many questions a teacher may rightly work out, such as why God made some things temporal and some eternal. Against it: Book 2, chapter 26, section 1 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103226.htm): "It is therefore better and more profitable to belong to the simple and unlettered class, and by means of love to attain to nearness to God". Book 2, chapter 28, section 7 leaves to God how matter was made and why some angels fell.

stances.summary: Thinking hard about God is good, but not for everyone, not in every setting and not on every point. It belongs to people who are being purified, at the right time and within limits.
stances.quote: Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God; not to every one; the Subject is not so cheap and low; and I will add, not before every audience, nor at all times, nor on all points; but on certain occasions, and before certain persons, and within certain limits.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Constantinople, 380, against the Eunomians, who treated God's being as a subject for clever debate. He is "the Theologian" and goes on to probe the Trinity in Orations 28-31, so this is about who and when, not whether. Section V in the NPNF numbering (27.4 in modern editions): "we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath". Section IX in the NPNF numbering (27.10 in modern editions) invites free thinking on lesser topics: "Philosophize about the world or worlds; about matter; about soul ... For in these subjects to hit the mark is not useless, and to miss it is not dangerous." He mocks those who make theology "a matter of pleasant gossip ... after the races, or the theatre".

stances.summary: Plunge into the mystery and keep going, though you will never reach the end. Yet faith would rather worship in silence, and only heretics force us to put such things into words.
stances.quote: Penetrate into the mystery, plunge into the darkness which shrouds that birth, where you will be alone with God the Unbegotten and God the Only-begotten. Make your start, continue, persevere. I know that you will not reach the goal, but I shall rejoice at your progress.
stances.translation: E. W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 356-360, much of it in exile in Phrygia for opposing Arianism. The next sentence: "For He who devoutly treads an endless road, though he reach no conclusion, will profit by his exertions." (New Advent prints "He" with a capital, though it means any seeker.) The same book, section 2, pulls the other way: "But the errors of heretics and blasphemers force us to deal with unlawful matters, to scale perilous heights, to speak unutterable words, to trespass on forbidden ground. Faith ought in silence to fulfil the commandments". Section 11: "the proper service of faith is to grasp and confess the truth that it is incompetent to comprehend its Object." Book 1 tells his own conversion as a long search for God.

stances.summary: The mind should keep travelling toward God, using each discovery as a step to the next. But the journey ends in faith, not in knowledge, because God is greater than anything we can know.
stances.quote: his mind, unimpeded by any object of sense, was never hindered from its journeying in quest of what lies beyond all that is known, but having gone by reasoning far beyond the wisdom of his countrymen
stances.translation: M. Day, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Against Eunomius (NPNF title: Answer to Eunomius' Second Book)
stances.location: The passage on Abraham (Book 2 in modern editions)
stances.context: c. 383, about Abraham as the model seeker. He goes on: Abraham used every idea of God "as supplies and appliances for his onward journey, ever making one discovery a stepping-stone to another". Then the turn: "it is impossible to draw near to God, unless faith mediate, and bring the seeking soul into union with the incomprehensible nature of God. For leaving behind him the curiosity that arises from knowledge, Abraham, says the Apostle, believed God". His Life of Moses teaches the same endless ascent, but has no public-domain English. A well-known satire of market-stall theology in Constantinople (the bread-seller who talks of "Begotten and Unbegotten") is usually cited from his sermon On the Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit; I did not check it.

stances.summary: Understanding of the faith should grow, in each person and in the whole Church, through the ages. But it must grow the way a body grows, staying the same faith and never turning into a different one.
stances.quote: But some one will say, perhaps, Shall there, then, be no progress in Christ's Church? Certainly; all possible progress. For what being is there, so envious of men, so full of hatred to God, who would seek to forbid it? Yet on condition that it be real progress, not alteration of the faith.
stances.translation: C. A. Heurtley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Lerins (southern Gaul), 434. Not in the candidate pool but a clear voice. The chapter continues that knowledge should "increase and make much and vigorous progress; but yet only in its own kind; that is to say, in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning." Chapter 22: "Let posterity welcome, understood through your exposition, what antiquity venerated without understanding." His famous rule of what has been believed "everywhere, always, by all" is the brake on this.

stances.summary: Searching out the meaning of Scripture is healthy and even cleans the heart. But the hidden things of God are learned by faith, and a mind that always examines is showing doubt and fear.
stances.quote: By faith we are instructed about those unattainable things, not by investigation and the power of knowledge.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh, Amsterdam, 1923
stances.location: Treatise 51 in Wensinck ("On the three degrees of knowledge"), p. 246
stances.context: Isaac, briefly bishop of Nineveh c. 676, a monk of the Church of the East (outside the Chalcedonian churches), much loved by the Orthodox. OCR text; the running head for this page is misread as "240". The same treatise: "Fear always accompanies doubt, and doubt examination, and investigation means, and means knowledge. And that which always examines and investigates, shows doubt and fear". It also says that at the highest stage "faith swallows knowledge, gives anew birth to it, wholly spiritual". On the other side, Treatise 1 (pp. 3-4): "There is nothing so apt to banish lascivious customs from the soul ... as burning for the love of teachings, and prosecuting investigations concerning the meaning of the words of the scriptures."

stances.summary: The mysteries of Scripture are meant to be understood. But you reach them by cleaning your heart and praying, not by piling up commentaries and arguments.
stances.quote: a monk who wanted to acquire a knowledge of the Scriptures ought not to spend his labour on the works of commentators, but rather to keep all the efforts of his mind and intentions of his heart set on purifying himself from carnal vices
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Marseilles, c. 420-425. Cassian reports this approvingly as the teaching of Abba Theodore, in indirect speech. It goes on: the mysteries "were not declared to us by the grace of the Holy Spirit in order that they should remain unknown and obscure; but they are rendered obscure by our fault". Chapter 33 tells how Theodore, faced with "some most difficult question", prayed seven days and nights until the answer was revealed. So questions are welcome, but they are answered by prayer and purity. Some of Cassian's views on grace were attacked in his lifetime by Prosper of Aquitaine.

stances.summary: If reason could explain God's works, they would not be wonderful, and faith would earn nothing. Yet Scripture is a river deep enough for an elephant to swim in, and it is meant to exercise the minds of the wise.
stances.quote: But we must know that God's work, if it is grasped by reason, is not wonderful; and faith has no merit where human reason supplies the proof.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (the only full English, Hurst 1990, is modern)
stances.original: Sed sciendum nobis est quod divina operatio, si ratione comprehenditur, non est admirabilis; nec fides habet meritum, cui humana ratio praebet experimentum.
stances.work: Forty Homilies on the Gospels (Homiliae in Evangelia)
stances.context: Rome, c. 591. The url is an OCR of Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 76. The OCR reads "Sed sciendum nobis est quod divina operatio si ratione comprehenditur, non cst adinirabilis; nec lides babet meritum, cui bu- mana ratio prrcbet e"xperimentum"; the original field gives the corrected Latin. It is about Christ passing through closed doors, and Gregory then reasons by analogy with the virgin birth, so it is not a ban on thought. Aquinas quotes it as an objection in Summa II-II, question 2, article 10 (https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3002.htm), in the Dominican Fathers' English: "there is no merit in believing what is shown by reason", and answers it. On the other side, the dedicatory letter to Leander before his Moralia on Job (Library of the Fathers translation, 1844, https://archive.org/download/moralsonbookofjo01greguoft/moralsonbookofjo01greguoft_djvu.txt): "as the word of God, by the mysteries which it contains, exercises the understanding of the wise, so usually by what presents itself on the outside, it nurses the simple-minded" (OCR hyphenates "simple- minded"), and Scripture is a river "wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large" (OCR has a margin word inside that sentence).

stances.summary: Knowing God is the highest goal there is. But real theology happens in prayer, not in argument.
stances.quote: If you are a theologian, you will pray truly. And if you pray truly, you are a theologian.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (English translations of On Prayer are modern)
stances.original: Εἰ θεολόγος εἶ, προσεύξῃ ἀληθῶς. καὶ εἰ ἀληθῶς προσεύχῃ, θεολόγος εἶ.
stances.context: Egyptian desert, late 4th century (died 399). The url is an OCR of the Greek Philokalia (Athens, 1893), which prints the work under the name of St Nilus the Ascetic; modern scholars give it to Evagrius. The OCR reads "Εἰ θεολόγος εἶ, προσεύξῃ ἀληθῶς. χαὶ ε ἀληθῶς προσεύχῃ, θεολόγος εἴ." with OCR slips. Heterodox status: Evagrius was a bold speculative thinker in the line of Origen, and his teachings were condemned with Origenism in 553. So he both probed very deeply and taught that the knowledge of God is reached in pure prayer. Weak fit for the quiz; use only with care.

stances.summary: Once you have the faith, stop searching. Curiosity beyond the rule of faith is where heresy comes from, and knowing nothing against the rule is knowing everything.
stances.quote: Let such curious art give place to faith; let such glory yield to salvation. At any rate, let them either relinquish their noisiness, or else be quiet. To know nothing in opposition to the rule (of faith), is to know all things.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.original: Cedat curiositas fidei, cedat gloria saluti. Certe aut non obstrepant aut quiescant. Aduersus regulam nihil scire omnia scire est.
stances.context: Carthage, c. 200, before his Montanist period (from c. 207). Latin checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praescrip.shtml. His concession, in the same chapter: "So long, however, as its form exists in its proper order, you may seek and discuss as much as you please, and give full rein to your curiosity", but "it is better for you to remain in ignorance, lest you should come to know what you ought not". Chapter 7: "We want no curious disputation after possessing Christ Jesus, no inquisition after enjoying the gospel! With our faith, we desire no further belief." Chapters 8-12 argue that "Seek, and you shall find" has a limit: "you have succeeded in finding when you have believed." Chapter 12 allows seeking that stays "within the rule of faith". He himself argued at great length about God (Against Praxeas). The learning topic uses his "Athens and Jerusalem" line from chapter 7.

stances.summary: Study God's creation as much as you like, but do not pry into God Himself. Prying and prayer cannot come from the same mouth.
stances.quote: Search out the sea, but search not out the Lord of the sea! I have seen the various who came down after me, when astonied, so that from the midst of the sea they returned to the dry ground; for a few moments they sustained it not. Who would linger and be searching on into the depths of the Godhead?
stances.translation: J. B. Morris, NPNF 2nd series vol. 13, 1898 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: The Pearl: Seven Hymns on the Faith (Hymns on Faith 81-87)
stances.context: Nisibis or Edessa, c. 360s, against the Arian "scrutinizers" of his day. Stanza 4: "Searching is mingled with thanksgiving ... Prayer and prying [come] from one mouth, and which shall we listen to?" Hymn 4, stanza 1: "The probing of the finger blinds the eye, and much more does that prying blind. the faith." (sic, stray full stop on the page). Hymn 7, stanza 1: "The Holy Ghost Who cannot be explored, they thought to explore with their questionings." He is not against thought: he is a deep theological poet who reads God in Scripture and in nature. His target is dissecting God's being.

stances.summary: Where there is faith, questions are not needed. Constant questioning undermines faith, because someone still searching has not yet found.
stances.quote: For where faith exists, there is no need of question. Where there is no room for curiosity, questions are superfluous. Questioning is the subversion of faith. For he that seeks has not yet found. He who questions cannot believe.
stances.translation: Oxford Library of the Fathers translation revised by Philip Schaff, NPNF 1st series vol. 13, 1889 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Late 4th century, preaching on Paul's warning against "endless genealogies, which minister questions". He meets the obvious objection: Christ's "Seek and you shall find" means prayer and longing, and he bids us "search the Scriptures, not to introduce the labors of questioning, but to end them". He is not against study: Homily 2 on Matthew, section 10 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200102.htm) scolds lay people for thinking "that the reading of the divine Scriptures appertains to those only [monks], when you need it much more than they." His homilies On the Incomprehensible Nature of God, against the Anomoeans, have only modern English.

stances.summary: You are told to believe, not given leave to cross-examine God. We may know that the Son is begotten, but it is not ours to dispute how.
stances.quote: No man calls in question one who is better than he is: to believe is enjoined upon you, without permission to question.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: On the Christian Faith (De fide), to the emperor Gratian
stances.context: Milan, 378-380, against Arian arguments. Book 1, chapter 10, section 65: "We are suffered to know that the Son is begotten, not to dispute upon the manner of His begetting. I cannot deny the one; the other I fear to search into". Section 64: "For me the knowledge of the mystery of His generation is more than I can attain to, — the mind fails, the voice is dumb". The learning topic uses his line against dialectic (Book 1, chapter 5, section 42).

stances.summary: About God, admitting how little we know is the best knowledge. Believe that God has a Son, and do not try to work out how.
stances.quote: For we explain not what God is but candidly confess that we have not exact knowledge concerning Him. For in what concerns God to confess our ignorance is the best knowledge.
stances.translation: Edwin Hamilton Gifford, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Jerusalem, c. 350, to people preparing for baptism. Not in the candidate pool. Lecture 11, section 19 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310111.htm): "This also believe, that God has a Son: but about the manner be not curious, for by searching you will not find." Lecture 11, section 13: "Be not ashamed to confess your ignorance, since you share ignorance with Angels." He still teaches about God: Lecture 6, section 5: "because I cannot drink up all the river, am I not even to take in moderation what is expedient for me?"

stances.summary: It is enough to know what Scripture tells us. Do not go on to ask how God made the world or how the Son was begotten.
stances.quote: Is it not enough for you to learn that God made the world, but do you also venture to ask whence He made it? Is it not enough for you to learn that the Son of God has been manifested to you for salvation if you believe, but do you also inquire curiously how He was begotten after the Spirit?
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, ANF vol. 5, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
stances.context: Rome, early 3rd century. Scholars debate whether this treatise is by the Hippolytus who wrote the Refutation of All Heresies. Section 9 says we learn about God "from the Holy Scriptures, and from no other source" and should discern things "Not according to our own will, nor according to our own mind". Section 10: "For us, then, it is sufficient simply to know that there was nothing contemporaneous with God."

stances.summary: The harder I tried to understand the Godhead of the Word, the further it slipped away. We cannot grasp what God is, only say what He is not, and I wrote only to refute error.
stances.quote: For the more I desired to write, and endeavoured to force myself to understand the Divinity of the Word, so much the more did the knowledge thereof withdraw itself from me; and in proportion as I thought that I apprehended it, in so much I perceived myself to fail of doing so.
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written 358-360, in hiding, sent with his account of the Arian persecution. Section 2: "I frequently designed to stop and to cease writing; believe me, I did." Also: "For although it be impossible to comprehend what God is, yet it is possible to say what He is not." He wrote only so that his silence would not "lead into impiety those who have made enquiry of you, and are given to disputation". A humble confession more than a ban, so strength 1. He spent his life in theological argument.

stances.summary: Saying "I do not know" about the deep things of God is the right road. When you want to know why God allows what He allows, attend to your own soul, because those are His judgments.
stances.quote: Abba Joseph saith, "I do not know." And Abba Anthony said unto him, "In truth, Abba Joseph, thou hast found the way to say, 'I do not know.'"
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Paradise, Of Humility)
stances.context: Egypt, 4th century (Antony died 356). The story: old men visit Antony; he asks each the meaning of "a word from the Book"; all try; Joseph says he does not know, and Antony praises him. The page is raw OCR that puts a space just inside some quotation marks: it reads Abba Joseph saith, " I do not know." ... to say, ' I do not know.' " so remove spaces next to quotation marks and collapse whitespace before comparing. The same book, saying 218, p. 199: Antony "besought God to inform him why young children died whilst so many old men lived, and why upright men were poor whilst the wicked were rich", and a voice answered: "Anthony, take care of thine own self, for these matters are the judgements of God." (In the OCR the quotation marks there are read as "44".) The words in that saying are the voice's, not Antony's. The Life of Antony by Athanasius (chapters 72-80) shows him telling philosophers that Christians persuade by faith rather than by Greek arguments; the learning topic quotes chapter 78.

stances.summary: I will not talk about heavenly mysteries. Ask me how to master the passions of your soul and I will gladly help.
stances.quote: He spake about the things which are above and concerning heavenly matters, but I can only talk about things which are below and about the things of earth; had he spoken to me about the passions of the soul I would have given him an answer; but since he talked about spiritual things, I know nothing about them.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Paradise)
stances.context: Egypt, 5th century. A famous visiting monk talks to Poemen "from the Scriptures concerning spiritual and heavenly things"; Poemen turns his face away and says nothing. The quote is his explanation. When the visitor then asks how to master his passions, Poemen welcomes him: "Open now thy mouth on such matters as these, and I will fill it with good things." The page is raw OCR. To compare: strip the stray quotation marks (and a stray "4") that begin continued lines, remove the running head "1 88 (Questions anfc Hnsvvers on tbe Hscettc 1Rule" that falls after "heavenly matters,", rejoin "pas- sions", and collapse whitespace. (The other scan, paradiseorgarden02ann, also runs "nothingabout" together.) The point is priorities, humility and practice, more than a rule against thinking.

stances.summary: The truth about God should be grasped by faith, not by reason. If faith came by argument, only philosophers and speakers would be saved, so follow the saints' authority instead.
stances.quote: For I had settled it firmly with myself that the truth of divine things must be grasped by faith rather than by reason. For if the faith of the holy Church were grasped by the reasoning of debate, and not by the devotion of belief, no one but philosophers and orators would possess blessedness.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (English of Augustine's Letter 119 is modern)
stances.original: Ego igitur cum apud memetipsum prorsus definierim, veritatem rei divinae ex fide magis quam ex ratione percipi oportere; si enim fides sanctae Ecclesiae ex disputationis ratione, non ex credulitatis pietate apprehenderetur, nemo praeter philosophos atque oratores beatitudinem possideret.
stances.context: c. 410. Not in the candidate pool. Consentius was a Christian layman and writer in the Balearic Islands. That site numbers its files one ahead: lettera_120_testo.htm holds Letter 119. He goes on: "non tam ratio requirenda de Deo, quam auctoritas est sequenda sanctorum" ("reason about God is not so much to be sought as the authority of the saints is to be followed"). Yet in the same letter he asks Augustine to explain the Trinity to him. Augustine's reply, Letter 120, tells him to "correct your definition" and says God does not hate our reason (see the Augustine entry). A ready-made pair for the quiz.

splits_fathers: Real voices stand on both sides, and almost nobody sits at either extreme. Nobody says "never think about God": even Tertullian allows seeking "within the rule of faith", and Chrysostom urges everyone to read Scripture. Nobody says "question everything": even Clement and Origen build on faith, and Augustine puts faith first. The real disagreements are four. (1) Order: must you believe before you probe (Augustine, Tertullian, Chrysostom), or may you weigh the truth for yourself first (Lactantius, Minucius Felix, Justin)? (2) Limits: are some things simply God's secret, such as His essence, how the Son is begotten, or why children die (Irenaeus, Cyril, Ambrose, Hippolytus, Antony, Ephrem, Basil on the essence)? Or is the unexplained left on purpose for us to explore (Origen, Hilary's "plunge into the darkness", Gregory of Nyssa's endless journey)? (3) Who: may anyone ask (Minucius Felix, Lactantius) or only the purified few at the right time (Gregory of Nazianzus, Boethius)? (4) How: by reasoning and debate (Clement, Origen, Boethius), or by prayer and a clean heart (Evagrius, Cassian, Isaac, Poemen)? The 4th-century Arian crisis pushed many Nicene writers to the cautious side, because they saw the Anomoeans treating God's being as a logic puzzle. The strongest "yes" voices are Alexandrian and early: Clement and Origen. The strongest "no" voices: Tertullian, Chrysostom (Homily 1 on 1 Timothy), Ambrose, Cyril, Ephrem, and the desert fathers.
splits_people_today: As the claim is worded, most people today would agree: questioning is widely seen as healthy, among the non-religious and among many Christians. Evangelical apologetics, the Catholic "faith and reason" tradition, and progressive talk of doubt and deconstruction all value questions, for different reasons. A real minority would disagree or hesitate: traditional and conservative believers who distrust speculation or see doubt as spiritual danger, and many Orthodox Christians who stress mystery and humility before God. Some sceptics would also say probing God is pointless rather than healthy. So the wording as given is one-sided today and would tell the quiz little. The four edges above split people better, especially: whether some questions about God should be left alone (the problem of suffering is the obvious one; Antony's saying), whether faith must come before questioning, and whether ordinary people or only experts should dig into hard doctrine.

misattributions.line: Credo quia absurdum (I believe because it is absurd)
misattributions.truth: Not in his works. The nearest is On the Flesh of Christ 5 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0315.htm), about the death of the Son of God: "it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd" (Latin: prorsus credibile est, quia ineptum est). It is a paradox about the Cross, not a rule against thinking. The slogan is a later coinage.

misattributions.line: Credo ut intelligam (I believe so that I may understand); also "Faith seeking understanding" (fides quaerens intellectum)
misattributions.truth: Both phrases are Anselm of Canterbury's, c. 1077-78: Proslogion 1, "Neque enim quaero intelligere ut credam, sed credo ut intelligam", and in its preface "Fides quaerens intellectum" was the book's first title (checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/anselmproslogion.html). Anselm drew them from Augustine. Augustine's own lines are "believe that you may understand" (Tractates on John 29.6) and "Faith seeks, understanding finds" (On the Trinity 15.2.2). Too late for this quiz, so quote Augustine's own words.

misattributions.line: Before He made the world, God was preparing hell for people who pry into mysteries
misattributions.truth: Augustine reports this as someone else's joke and refuses it: Confessions 11.12.14 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/110111.htm), "I answer not, as a certain person is reported to have done facetiously ... He was preparing hell, says he, for those who pry into mysteries." He would rather say "I know not" than mock "him who asks deep things". Using it as his view reverses his meaning.

misattributions.line: Is not this truly the duty of philosophy, to investigate the Deity?
misattributions.truth: In Dialogue with Trypho 1 this question is spoken by Trypho, the Jewish speaker. Justin only answers "Assuredly, so we too have believed." Credit the question to Trypho.

misattributions.line: What is above us is nothing to us
misattributions.truth: In the Octavius (chapter 13) this is the pagan Caecilius quoting Socrates to argue that Christians should not dispute about heavenly things. The Christian speaker, Octavius, rejects it in chapters 16-17.

This comes from the pagan critic Celsus (c. 175), as quoted by Origen in Against Celsus 1.9 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm). It is a hostile report of what some Christians said, not a Christian's own writing. Origen grants that simple faith helps the many but denies that it is the Christian ideal.

misattributions.line: If you are a theologian, you will pray truly
misattributions.truth: The Philokalia (Greek, 1893) prints On Prayer under the name of Nilus the Ascetic. Modern scholarship gives it to Evagrius Ponticus. Credit Evagrius, and note the Philokalia attribution if needed.

notes: All quotations were copied from raw pages fetched with curl and checked as exact substrings after collapsing whitespace, except the three own renderings (Gregory the Great, Evagrius, Consentius), whose original-language text was checked instead. The Augustine entry also gives my rendering of Letter 120 in context. Budge and Wensinck pages are OCR text: the quotes match the OCR exactly, and clean readings are given in context where the OCR has stray marks. Lines not used because they could not be verified here: Gregory of Nyssa's bread-seller satire (On the Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit); Augustine, Sermon 117 ("if you comprehend it, it is not God"); John Climacus (no pre-1929 English found). No clear statements on this question were found for Ignatius, Perpetua, Cyprian, Novatian, Martin of Tours, Paulinus of Nola, Benedict, Pelagius, Amma Syncletica, Moses the Black or Arsenius; Arsenius's "alphabet of this villager" saying is about worldly learning and sits in the learning topic. Overlap with the learning topic (Athens and Jerusalem, pagan philosophy) was avoided: this topic is about probing God and doctrine, and different passages were chosen for Tertullian, Ambrose, Antony and Boethius. Strong reveal pairs: Clement against Tertullian; Augustine against Consentius (the same exchange of letters); Hilary's "plunge into the darkness" against Chrysostom's "Questioning is the subversion of faith"; Minucius Felix ("any one should inquire") against Gregory of Nazianzus ("Not to every one"). Reverent capitals: the NPNF and ANF texts mostly capitalise pronouns for God, but not always (Clement, Basil and others print "His" inconsistently, and older translations sometimes lower-case). Leave them as printed for the machine check and apply the house style only at display time, if the site's rule allows that.
